Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette:
Carlos was fifty-four years old when he finally walked into a therapist's office, though he had been carrying the weight of that decision for nearly a decade. He was a business owner now-a small grocery store in a working-class Latino neighborhood in Houston-but before that, he had spent two years as a relief worker in a war-torn region of Central America. The memory that owned him was not a long, drawn-out ordeal but a single, fractured moment. He had been driving a supply truck through a dusty village, and a child had darted into the road. He slammed the brakes, and for a split second there was relief-the boy was safe, Carlos had stopped in time-and then the gunfire came. A single shot, impossibly loud, from somewhere behind a collapsed wall. The boy fell. Carlos never saw who fired. He scrambled out, tried to apply pressure, but the child was already gone. What stayed with him wasn't just the sound, but the sudden switch from that brief, warm feeling of having averted disaster to the cold, irreversible reality of the shot. That moment of positive emotion-the fleeting happiness that he had not hit the boy-became an unbearable betrayal in hindsight.

After he returned to the United States, Carlos tried to pick up his old life. He married, bought the grocery store, and told himself it was all behind him. But the triggers were everywhere. A car backfiring on the street sent him diving behind a display of canned beans, heart hammering. More puzzling to him was what happened during good times. At his own wedding reception, when his wife laughed and pulled him onto the dance floor, he felt a wave of nausea. The joy felt dangerous, like a trap that could be shattered at any moment. He began to avoid celebrations. Holidays, birthdays, even a quiet evening with his wife when she looked too happy-he would make an excuse, walk away, start an argument. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel good, something terrible would follow. It was a superstition he could not shake, and so he started picking fights. It was easier to feel angry than to wait for the other shoe to drop. His wife, Marta, accused him of being impossible, of looking for reasons to fight. He knew she was right, but he could not stop. The arguments gave him a focused, immediate pain that drowned out the older, deeper one.

He also began to carry a weapon. At first it was a small pistol in his glove compartment, then one in his jacket pocket, then a second one under the counter at the store. He knew it was not legal to carry concealed in the store without a license-he had one for his truck-but the thought of being unarmed made him feel as though he were naked and surrounded. He was certain that the same kind of violence could find him here, in a busy corner store in Houston. Every customer who came too close, who reached into a bag or turned too quickly, made his hand twitch toward his hip. He had developed an acute sensitivity to physical proximity. Strangers standing near him in line, a hand on his shoulder from a friend-his body reacted before his mind could catch up. He had stopped shaking hands, stopped hugging his own nephews.

At night, alone in the back office after closing, Carlos would replay the event. He went over and over the moment, asking himself why it had happened to him, what he could have done differently, why he was spared when a six-year-old boy was not. He could not find an answer, only a deepening sense that he was marked, that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he alone had to be on guard. The rumination ate up hours. He slept poorly, drank more than he should, and snapped at Marta until she stopped trying to comfort him.

The consequence that finally brought him to seek help was a lost contract. A supplier he had worked with for years pulled out after he yelled at their delivery driver for standing too close. The driver had been a young man, maybe twenty, and when he leaned in to hand Carlos a clipboard, Carlos shoved him backward and screamed at him to back off. The driver quit, the supplier complained, and Carlos lost a major account. Marta told him that night, through tears, that she could not keep living this way. He knew he could not either. What frightened him most was the idea that if he stopped being vigilant, stopped carrying the weapon, stopped the arguments, he would be helpless-that the boy's death would finally catch up to him, or that his own happiness would invite another shot. But something in Marta's voice made him call the number she had left on the table. He wanted, more than anything, to sleep through a night without the sound of that gunshot.
